description: Language-neutral conformance vectors for the euRedact rule engine. Both the Python and the TypeScript SDK run these, so cross-SDK parity is a test rather than an assumption. Each case is input plus an expectation; no language-specific detail belongs here.

schema.countries: list of ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 codes, or null for no country hint
schema.mustDetect: map of entity type -> exact list of detected texts for that type, in document order
schema.mustNotDetect: list of entity types that must produce no detection
schema.options: optional per-call options, camelCase as in the TypeScript RedactOptions; today `allowlist` (values never to redact) and `allowlistDomains` (domains whose addresses are never redacted)
schema.expectRedactedText: optional exact redacted output; the default bracketed labels, with no referential or token option

cases.notes: The key body must not absorb the slashes in front of it. Anchoring the high-entropy rule with a class lookbehind instead of \b widened the span leftwards over them; the result matched the protocol-relative URL shape the endpoint suppressor drops, and the key was left in the clear.

Αρ. Ταυτότητας is Greek for 'ID number' and is official on a Cypriot identity document. No Cypriot pattern matches a bare 8-digit ID, so the span was claimed by a Finnish phone rule; the cue relabels it.

Greece's ΑΦΜ is issued by the tax authority; the identity-document number is the ΑΔΤ. The value failed the AFM checksum, so the Greek rule declined and a Czech birth-number pattern that happened to validate took the span.
One qualifier word may sit between the label and the colon.
The Romanian postal candidate existed and passed its context gate, but postal codes rank below everything by design, so a German phone pattern won. A cue outranks priority.
The canon annotates INTERNAL_ID with an LLM, so the engine has no pattern for one — but it had a phone pattern that claimed it. Emitted from the cue alone.

Strengthens be-invalid-nrn-is-not-a-phone, which asserts only that this is not a PHONE — and passed for four releases while the engine emitted nothing at all, printing in full an identifier it had recognised and rejected. A declined identifier with its own label in front of it is still that identifier.
Re-typing is gated to generic numeric shapes. EMAIL carries its own structure and a nearby word may not overrule it.
The VAT cue had no left boundary, so 'iva' matched inside 'Privat'. Same class of defect as 'NIS' matching the tail of 'tālrunis'.
653 Latvian phone numbers were once suppressed because 'NIS' matched the tail of 'tālrunis'. The boundary that fixed it moved into the cue table with the label.

A cue label may run on into a longer word, or take one qualifier word — never both. Allowing both let 'nie' grow into 'Nieminen' and then swallow the real 'DOB' label, reading 52 dates of birth across the corpus as Spanish NIEs.

The rescue applies to checksummed identifiers, not registry lookups. A BIC validator failure means 'no such bank', which a label cannot talk you out of; rescuing it read 34 unlisted codes as real ones.
VAT labels carry punctuation inside the run-on, so that cue keeps a wider run-on class than the rest.
Spelled-out UK register label. 0.3.8 typed this PHONE.
Three words. The tail allows a run-on OR one qualifier, never a second word, so the label is spelled out in the table.
The abbreviation BSN was cued; the word it abbreviates was not.
Closing parenthesis between label and value. Also needed CUE_WINDOW past 22.
Was in the cue table throughout 0.3.8 and unreachable: at 27 characters the label did not fit CUE_WINDOW=22, so its own start fell outside the window where the boundary anchors.
Two trailing marks, and the winner was a Czech NATIONAL_ID whose checksum passed with zero Czech evidence in the document.
The clinician, not the patient: distinct from HEALTH_INSURANCE.
No colon. A label without one is still a label.
NN-NN-NN collides with a licence-plate shape, and 0.3.8 typed it LICENSE_PLATE with the label in front of it.
Typed SECRET: this SDK has no CREDENTIAL type.
Abbreviating full stop, no colon. Reported as a Czech NATIONAL_ID by Python and a Portuguese PHONE by Node.

issue rules-engine#5: the tail after '::' used to survive into the output ('[IPV6_ADDRESS]ff00:42:8329'). Alternation is leftmost-first, so the branch that consumes most must be ordered first.
issue rules-engine#5: not detected at all before, because the pattern anchored on \b and ':' is a non-word character.
The port is not part of the address; the brackets stay.

issue rules-engine#5: the IPv4 rule used to claim the quad and leave '::ffff:' in the clear. Every group of a dotted quad is also valid hex, so the IPv4-embedded branches must precede the hex branches.
A trailing sentence period must neither truncate the address nor be swallowed by it.
A bare '::' is the unspecified address, not an identifier; matching it would redact the C++/Rust scope operator.
Colon-separated hex that is not an IPv6 address must stay with its own type.
issue rules-engine#3: the closing parenthesis of the surrounding text used to join the span, giving 'Call ([PHONE] today.'
The parenthesised trunk prefix is what the optional parentheses were written for; pairing them must not lose it.
issue rules-engine#10: the local-part class had no apostrophe, so the match began after it and masked as "johno'[EMAIL]" — the surname stayed in the clear. 1,415 corpus entities.
The apostrophe belongs to the surrounding text here. Putting ' in the character class would have absorbed it, the same defect as rules-engine#3.
A possessive near an address must not extend the span.
issue rules-engine#15: separators in a structured identifier are presentational, so an allowlisted IBAN is exempt however the document spaces it.
Folding widens the spelling, never the scope: a different account is still redacted.
issue rules-engine#17: an owned domain, without enumerating every mailbox.
The match is on a label boundary: acme.be must not exempt evilacme.be.
issue rules-engine#23: the shape is not German and the label is not Dutch, so before the shared keyword list neither pattern fired. A foreign passport in a German document is the ordinary case.
The generic shape is only safe because it is label-gated; without a passport word it must never fire.
Context matching is substring, so the bare Scandinavian 'pass' would fire inside 'password'. It is deliberately absent from the keyword list; only compound forms are listed.
A conforming German passport is still matched; the generic rule ranks below the national one and does not displace it.
